newsitem.title: FRANCE: Fiscal rigour not to blame for jobless - EU chief.
newsitem.headline: Fiscal rigour not to blame for jobless - EU chief.

text.p: European Union President Jacques Santer, defending the tough budgetary discipline required for creating a single European currency, said on Thursday that fiscal rigour was not to blame for high unemployment.
"It's wrong to believe (fiscal) rigour brings recession and unemployment," he told the French national assembly's foreign affairs committee.
"Those member states which have made strides in cutting their deficits have seen good results in job creation. Take the Netherlands, Denmark, Ireland (for example)," Santer said.

His pep talk came on the same day as the release of figures showing another 27,700 people had joined France's jobless rolls -- almost double the amount forecast by economists -- pushing the country's unemployment rate to a record 12.6 percent.
Santer added he was convinced monetary union would be a powerful force for economic growth but said advocates would have to do a better sales job to convince the public.
Countries needed to step up efforts to promote employment in order to dispel cynicism and gloom about monetary union among Europeans, he said.

"Europe cannot ignore the biggest worry (unemployment) of its citizens," he said, adding that people were saying the drive toward greater European integration was "failing to lower unemployment and not achieving anything any more."

Some critics of a single currency say the budget tightening required to cut deficits to qualify for monetary union is stifling economic growth and is responsible for high jobless rates plaguing many European countries.

Santer has been pushing hard for the European Union to spend more than $1 billion on trans-European road and rail projects to boost employment. But those proposals were rejected again by EU finance ministers last week.

Santer reiterated his belief that European economic and monetary union (EMU) would come into effect as targeted on January 1, 1999, and that a "substantial number of member states would participate in monetary union from the start."
He added that he believed progress would be made at next month's European Council meeting in Dublin towards creating a "stability pact" to ensure lasting budget discipline among EMU members.

Santer also stressed that it was vital that EU institutions be reformed before the wealthy bloc absorbs an influx of new, poorer members. Otherwise, he said, the process would become too unwieldy. "We must do the necessary reforms now."
